title: PriFi: Securing the Entire Transaction Supply Chain | Logos
description: PriFi (Private Finance) secures every step of the transaction supply chain, not just settlement. Learn the 7-step transaction lifecycle, the two hazard classes, and why blockchain's transparency creates new risks.

heading: A parallel society needs an economy.
PriFi protects its participants.
body: PriFi, or private finance, is a technical design philosophy: financial primitives deployed on privacy-preserving, peer-to-peer infrastructure, on hardware you control.
Strengthening commitments to reduce transaction costs by limiting what an attacker can learn about a transaction and what they can manipulate.
Purpose-built for privacy and security, not patches "bolted on" later.

supplyChain.heading: The transaction supply chain
supplyChain.tabListLabel: The links of the transaction supply chain
supplyChain.lead: Settlement is just one of seven links in the chain. Blockchain provides unprecedented settlement security. But transactions depend on infrastructure beyond settlement. Every exposed link creates another opportunity for privacy leaks or manipulation. Increased risk means increased transaction costs.
supplyChain.note: PriFi protects participants from two directions: limiting what an attacker can learn and what they can influence. Leaks cost billions annually. Even small efficiency increases add up: a 0.1% drop in transaction costs can quadruple a nation's wealth.

links.label: 01 Discovery
links.body: Finding a counterparty who has what you want.
links.tools: Browsers, order books, RFQ platforms, direct messages, block explorers, wallets leaking IPs, globally linkable identity graphs via fingerprinting.
links.threat: Onchain analysis maps wallets and flows before a deal exists.

links.label: 02 Diligence
links.body: Verifying they are who they claim.
links.tools:
Browsers, wallets leaking IPs, globally linkable identity graphs via fingerprinting.

Onchain analytics, attestations, reserve and credit checks.
links.threat: In offchain finance, a counterparty can misrepresent reserves. Onchain, an outsider can watch diligence requests, infer intent, and identify targets before terms are even set.

links.label: 03 Negotiation
links.tools: Chat apps, RFQ threads, term sheets, public mempools.
links.threat:
Leaked terms let an attacker position themselves ahead of transaction execution.

A counterparty can stall or renegotiate once terms are known elsewhere.

links.label: 04 Contracting
links.exposes: Wallet addresses, browser-derived data, approximate location, signing contexts.
links.tools: Browsers, wallets leaking IP, globally linkable identity graphs via fingerprinting, DNS, IPFS, AWS, RPCs, and other centralised frontends create billion-dollar attack surfaces.
links.threat:
A spoofed signing interface can show one transaction and execute another.

The signer authorises something they never agreed to.

graph.alt: Contracting. The interface can lie. The signature can't take it back.

links.label: 05 Ordering
links.exposes: IPs, pending order flow, intent, sizing, timing.
links.threat:
A visible mempool tells every bot watching exactly what's about to happen.

Frontrunning and sandwich attacks run on that visibility.

graph.alt: Ordering. Public order flow exposes transactions to frontrunning.

links.label: 06 Settlement
links.body: The only link where value moves.
links.tools: RPC endpoints, wallets, browsers, relayer networks.
links.threat:
The blockchain finalises exactly what reaches settlement, including upstream compromises.

It enforces what was signed, not necessarily what was intended.

stats.note: stolen through forged SWIFT payment instructions.

graph.alt: Settlement. The chain executes exactly what it's given.

links.label: 07 Enforcement and recourse
links.body: Making the outcome stick, or proving what happened when it does not.
links.exposes: Proposer and validator addresses, staking balances, transactions validated, transactor wallet addresses.
links.tools: Browsers, wallets leaking IPs, globally linkable identity graphs via fingerprinting, onchain analytics.
links.threat:
Blockchain finality makes transactions difficult to reverse, even if it was not the intended transaction. Recourse moves outside the protocol, where dispute resolution requires exposing everything.

External pressure on identifiable validators to censor transactions compromises blockchain sovereignty.

stats.note: Breaking offshore and Swiss banking secrecy introduced $2B+ in enforcement costs.

graph.alt: Enforcement and recourse. Dispute resolution exposes transaction participants and validators.

lines: Each exposed link is an opportunity for exploitation.
Secure one link and the attacker moves to the next.
exploitBand.conclusion: PriFi aims to protect the whole transaction supply chain.

hazards.heading: Two hazard classes: The counterparty and the outsider

classes.name: THE COUNTERPARTY
classes.who: The person or institution you're transacting with
classes.risk: Counterparties need information to make a deal possible, creating opportunities for misrepresentation, concealment, default, or other opportunism.
classes.bound: Able to exploit information made available by necessity, but bound by the deal's terms.

classes.name: THE OUTSIDER
classes.risk: Thieves and extortionists can target your holdings and what you can pay. Frontrunners and competitors can exploit your positions and intentions.
classes.bound: Outsiders are not party to the transaction. They signed nothing and cannot be bound by its terms, only denied exploitable information.

protection.heading: Two forms of protection: Security and privacy
protection.lead: The two hazard classes require different defences.
body: Security binds, making defection difficult or costly.
Privacy starves, denying information needed to identify, target, or exploit a transaction.

cells.reason: Inside the transaction and can be made subject to its rules and commitments. Security reduces their ability or incentive to misrepresent, default, or defect.
A transaction requires some information to pass between counterparties. You can minimise what is disclosed, but you cannot remove the counterparty's access to the deal entirely.
Entered no agreement with you. There may be no contract, collateral, or protocol commitment capable of constraining what they do with information they obtain.
An outsider must first find something worth exploiting. Concealing counterparties, holdings, positions, and intentions removes the information needed to identify and attack a target.

transparency.heading: Institutional quality is measured by the credibility of the commitments they make
transparency.body:
Transactions depend on promises about future behaviour. Promises that are dependable when breaking them becomes attractive are known as credible commitments.

The stronger those commitments, the less participants need to spend verifying, monitoring, insuring against, or policing one another.

The credibility of commitments can fall into two categories: motivational and imperative.

credibility.title: Motivational credibility
body: A party can break a commitment, but has a reason not to.
The commitment holds for as long as the incentives to keep it do.

credibility.title: Imperative credibility
body: The discretion to defect is removed structurally.
The system makes violating the commitment prohibitively costly.
credibility.note: Blockchains introduced imperative credibility for transaction settlement by making rules self-enforcing.

imperativeCommitments.heading: Imperative commitments reduce the cost of transacting
imperativeCommitments.body: When participants have structural assurances, rather than trust alone, risk mitigation costs fall. Lower transaction costs enable new market activity.

logosStack.heading: Logos protects the full transaction supply chain
logosStack.body: A complete, unified stack providing unprecedented imperative credibility at every link.

rows.role: A self-contained desktop application that bundles everything you need to interact with the Logos stack. A UI running locally on user-controlled hardware.
Anonymous communication and coordination. Stops intentions leaking before terms exist.

Decentralised content-addressed storage commits a content hash to the exact file or interface being retrieved: alter the content, and the hash changes. Instead of trusting a server, the integrity of what you load can be verified independently.
Consensus-aware private propagation obscures where transactions and block proposals originate, disrupting ordering observation and exploitation.
Private PoS keeps those securing settlement from becoming targets for bribery, coercion, or censorship.
Programmable privacy makes disclosure selective. Participants can prove what is needed for compliance or dispute resolution without exposing entire transaction histories.

institutions.heading: What institutions sold to a few, PriFi makes structural.
body: Security and privacy have historically been expensive institutional services available through trusted intermediaries and favourable jurisdictions. PriFi extends access to anyone with an online device.

Logos infrastructure elevates institutional commitments from strong motivational to structurally imperative to provide even greater protections than those that were previously reserved only for the ultra wealthy.
